fluid-flow-s1.title: Water in a narrowing pipe
fluid-flow-s1.text: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) flows steadily through a horizontal pipe that narrows from section 1 to section 2. The pipe is full and the water is an ideal fluid.

fluid-flow-s2.title: A tank with a hole
fluid-flow-s2.html: The tank is much wider than the hole, and the water is an ideal fluid. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

items.q: What is the volume flow rate of the water? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided area by speed. Volume flow rate is area × speed, Av.

why.correct: Volume flow rate = A₁v₁ = (4.0 × 10⁻³ m²)(1.5 m/s) = 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³/s, six liters each second. It is the same at every section of the pipe.

items.q: What is the speed of the water at section 2? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the ratio is upside down. The water must speed up where the pipe is narrower: v₂ = v₁A₁/A₂.
Value: the speed changes. The same volume each second must pass through a smaller area: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.

why.correct: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = (4.0 × 10⁻³ m²)(1.5 m/s)/(1.0 × 10⁻³ m²) = 6.0 m/s. A quarter of the area, four times the speed.

items.q: What is the absolute pressure at section 2? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the sign is reversed. Where the water moves faster, its pressure is lower: P₂ = P₁ + ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²).
Value: you left out the ½ in the kinetic term. Bernoulli uses ½ρv².
Value: you used ½ρ(Δv)². Use the difference of the squares: ½ρ(v₁² − v₂²).

why.correct: Bernoulli with y₁ = y₂ (horizontal pipe): P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂². P₂ = 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa + ½(1000 kg/m³)[(1.5 m/s)² − (6.0 m/s)²] = 2.00 × 10⁵ Pa − 1.69 × 10⁴ Pa = 1.83 × 10⁵ Pa.

items.q: A student predicts that the pressure is higher at section 2 because the water is squeezed into a narrower pipe. Which response is correct?
options: Lower at section 2: the water speeds up there, so it is pushed from behind
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the narrow walls push in on the water
The pressure is the same at both sections, because the water is incompressible
The pressure is higher at section 2, because the same flow rate passes through less area

why.correct: Water speeds up from section 1 to section 2, so it gains kinetic energy. A net force must act on it in the direction of flow, which means the pressure behind it (section 1) is larger than the pressure ahead (section 2).
options: Right: faster flow, lower pressure in a horizontal pipe.
This "squeezing" picture is the classic error; the water accelerates into the narrow part, so the pressure there is lower.
Incompressible means constant density, not constant pressure.
The same flow rate through less area means higher speed, which goes with lower pressure.

items.q: Which principle sets the speed at section 2, and which sets the pressure there?
options: Continuity sets the speed; Bernoulli then sets the pressure
Bernoulli sets the speed; continuity then sets the pressure
Bernoulli alone sets both, with no need for continuity
Continuity alone sets both, because the pipe is horizontal

why.correct: The volume flowing in each second must flow out (an incompressible fluid cannot pile up), so A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ gives v₂ from the areas alone. Bernoulli, an energy statement, then turns the speed change into a pressure change.
options: Right: geometry and continuity first, then energy.
Bernoulli has two unknowns here (P₂ and v₂); continuity has to supply the speed.
One equation cannot give two unknowns.
Continuity says nothing about pressure.

items.q: What is the speed of the water as it leaves the hole? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: that is v². Take the square root: v = √(2gh).
Value: you lost the factor of 2. ρgh = ½ρv² gives v = √(2gh).

why.correct: Bernoulli from the surface (point 1) to the hole (point 2): both are open to the air, so P₁ = P₂ = P₀; the surface barely moves, so v₁ ≈ 0. Then ρgy₁ = ρgy₂ + ½ρv², and v = √(2g × 1.8 m) = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.8) m/s = 5.9 m/s (Torricelli's result).

items.q: Why can the speed of the water surface in the tank be taken as zero?
options: By continuity, the wide surface moves far more slowly than the water in the small hole
The water at the surface is at atmospheric pressure, so it does not move
The surface is the highest point, so its kinetic energy is converted to potential energy
The water in the tank is at rest; just the jet moves

why.correct: A_surface v_surface = A_hole v_hole. With A_surface much larger than A_hole, v_surface is tiny, and ½ρv² there is negligible.
options: Right: continuity makes the surface speed negligible.
Pressure does not stop motion; the surface is falling, just slowly.
The surface does not gain or lose height quickly; this is not why its speed is small.
The water level is dropping, so the water in the tank moves; just slowly.

items.q: A second hole is made 7.2 m below the surface of a taller tank of the same kind. How does the jet speed from this hole compare with the 1.8 m hole?
options: Twice as fast
Four times as fast
√2 times as fast
The same

why.correct: v = √(2gh), so v ∝ √h. Four times the depth (7.2/1.8 = 4) gives √4 = 2 times the speed.
options: Right: speed grows as the square root of depth.
This treats v as proportional to h; it is proportional to √h.
The depth is 4 times as large, not 2 times.
Deeper water is at higher pressure and pushes the jet out faster.

items.q: The hole is replaced by one with half the area, at the same depth. What happens to the jet's speed and to the volume flow rate out of the hole?
options: Speed unchanged; flow rate halved
Speed doubled; flow rate unchanged
Speed halved; flow rate halved
Speed doubled; flow rate doubled

why.correct: The exit speed √(2gh) depends only on the depth, not on the hole's size. The flow rate Av then halves with A.
options: Right: v from depth, then flow rate = Av.
A garden-hose nozzle speeds water up because a pump keeps the flow rate fixed; here the depth fixes the speed instead.
Nothing about the speed formula involves the hole's area.
The speed is set by the depth; with less area the flow rate cannot grow.

items.q: The hole has an area of 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². What is the volume flow rate out of it? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you used v² in place of v. Find v = √(2gh) first, then multiply by the area.

why.correct: Flow rate = Av = (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²)(5.94 m/s) = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³/s, about 1.2 liters per second.

items.q: You put your thumb over part of the end of a garden hose, and the water sprays out faster. Why?
options: The same volume per second leaves through a smaller area
Your thumb adds energy to the water as it squeezes past
The pressure at the end rises, which slows the water inside the hose
Water is compressed under your thumb and expands as it leaves

why.correct: The supply pushes water through at about the same volume flow rate. Continuity, Av = constant, means a smaller opening needs a larger speed.
options: Right: continuity.
Your thumb is at rest, so it does no work on the water.
Inside the hose the water slows slightly; the faster jet is outside, at lower pressure.
Water is nearly incompressible; continuity, not compression, explains the jet.

items.q: Treat blood as an ideal fluid. It flows at 0.30 m/s in an artery. At a narrowed section, the area is one third of the normal area. What is the blood's speed in the narrowed section? Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: the speed goes up where the area goes down. v₂ = v₁(A₁/A₂) = 3 × 0.30 m/s.

why.correct: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ with A₂ = A₁/3, so v₂ = 3v₁ = 0.90 m/s.

items.q: Water flows at a steady speed up a vertical pipe of constant cross section. What is the difference in pressure between two points 5.0 m apart in height? Use g = 9.8 m/s² and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Give the value and its unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you left out g. The pressure difference is ρgΔy.
Value: there is no ½ here. With equal speeds the kinetic terms cancel, leaving P₁ − P₂ = ρg(y₂ − y₁).

why.correct: Continuity: constant area means equal speeds, so the ½ρv² terms cancel in Bernoulli's equation. P_low − P_high = ρgΔy = (1000 kg/m³)(9.8 m/s²)(5.0 m) = 4.9 × 10⁴ Pa; the lower point has the higher pressure.

items.q: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of which conservation law, applied to a moving fluid?
options: Conservation of energy
Conservation of mass
Conservation of momentum
Conservation of angular momentum

why.correct: Each term is an energy per unit volume: ½ρv² (kinetic), ρgy (gravitational potential), and P (the work done per unit volume by the pressure pushing the fluid along). With no friction (an ideal fluid), their sum stays constant along the flow.
options: Right: energy per unit volume.
Mass conservation is the continuity equation, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Momentum conservation is not what Bernoulli expresses.
Bernoulli involves no rotation.

items.q: Water flows through a full horizontal pipe that widens to twice its diameter. Predict how each quantity in the wide part compares with the narrow part.

variables.name: Volume flow rate
variables.why: Continuity: what flows in each second flows out; the fluid is incompressible.

variables.name: Speed of the water
variables.why: Twice the diameter is four times the area, so the speed is a quarter as large.

variables.name: Pressure in the water
variables.why: Bernoulli, same height: the water slows down, so its pressure rises.

why.correct: Continuity sets the speeds from the areas; Bernoulli then gives the pressure change.

items.q: A smooth stream of water falling from a faucet gets narrower as it falls. Which explanation is correct?
options: It speeds up as it falls, so by continuity its area shrinks
Air pressure squeezes the stream more and more as it falls
The water is compressed by its own weight as it falls
Some water evaporates from the stream, so less is left

why.correct: Gravity speeds the water up. The volume flow rate Av is the same at every height, so where v is larger, A must be smaller.
options: Right: faster flow, smaller area.
Air pressure is about the same all along the short stream.
Water is nearly incompressible.
Evaporation over a fraction of a second is negligible.
